## Original idea
{
  "title": "GatedRubric-GRPO: Continuous Hierarchical Gating with Decoupled Normalization for Non-Verifiable Multimodal Scientific Reasoning",
  "core_problem": "Reinforcement learning with structured rewards has advanced rapidly across three converging axes: (1) gated/hierarchical rewards for verifiable multimodal tasks (PaLMR, PEARL, CogFlow use binary visual gates; VGPO uses a binary Visual Gate for attention compensation), (2) rubric-based RL for non-verifiable tasks (RaR [ICLR 2026] uses rubric rewards with GRPO for medicine/science; DRO uses binary rubric-gates as feasibility constraints; Training AI Co-Scientists applies rubric RL to scientific plan generation), and (3) perception-aware VLM training (VPPO, PAPO, From Seeing to Thinking [ICML 2026] demonstrate perception-first training is critical; Bad Seeing or Bad Thinking [ICML 2026] introduces MoCA for perception-reasoning credit assignment; Perceval integrates claim-level perception verification into RL training via token-level advantage modulation). However, ALL existing gating mechanisms in RL training — whether for visual fidelity (PaLMR), rubric feasibility (DRO), essential criteria qualification (rDPO), visual attention compensation (VGPO), or Lagrangian visual grounding constraints (FGRPO) — employ BINARY or DISCRETE constraint mechanisms: hard accept/reject, pass/fail, or threshold-based Lagrangian penalties. Separately, works exploring continuous alternatives to binary rewards have shown strong empirical benefits: ReDit demonstrates 10× faster convergence when adding noise to make discrete rewards continuous (with formal optimization time bounds in Theorem 1); Gradient Starvation in Binary-Reward GRPO shows 69% of GRPO groups become degenerate (zero-advantage) with binary rewards at group size 4; and Smooth Operator demonstrates that sigmoid-shaped continuous rewards improve VLM GRPO by +5.6% over binary baselines when combined with absolute-preserving advantage estimation (AP-GRPO). Furthermore, GDPO (ICML 2026) proves that naive GRPO normalization of multi-reward aggregation causes distinct reward combinations to collapse into identical advantage values — directly relevant when composite rewards combine multiple gated tiers. Meanwhile, Grounding the Score uses the sigmoid formula α(r)=σ(β(r−τ)) for inference-time calibration of visual reliability in process reward models — the same functional form we propose for RL training. The problem is especially acute for non-verifiable scientific visual reasoning — tasks like scientific figure explanation, graph-based analytical interpretation, and figure critique — where both visual grounding quality and reasoning quality are INHERENTLY CONTINUOUS and GRADED. A figure can be 70% correctly perceived; a scientific explanation can be partially valid. Binary gating and discrete constraint mechanisms discard this graded signal.",
  "opportunity": "The landscape reveals a specific technical gap at the intersection of five established directions, each now well-validated independently. Direction 1: Gated multimodal rewards exist (PaLMR, PEARL, CogFlow, VGPO) but use binary gates on verifiable tasks. FGRPO uses Lagrangian dual ascent for visual grounding constraints — a principled alternative to gating — but its Table 2 reveals that naive binary multiplicative gating DEGRADES accuracy by −1.7pp while inconsistency remains at 19.6%, because binary masking eliminates gradient signal from gated components. Direction 2: Rubric-based non-verifiable RL is now established — RaR (ICLR 2026) demonstrates up to 31% improvement on medical reasoning with rubric rewards via GRPO, but uses flat weighted aggregation without gating or hierarchical structure. DRO uses binary rubric-gates but is text-only. Direction 3: Perception-aware VLM training is validated — From Seeing to Thinking (ICML 2026) proves that 86.9% of VLM errors stem from perception failures and that perception-first staged training yields +4.6pp improvement; Bad Seeing or Bad Thinking (ICML 2026) shows MoCA credit assignment between perception and reasoning; PAPO finds 67% of failures from perception errors; Perceval demonstrates claim-level error grounding with token-level RL integration for perception. Direction 4: Continuous rewards/gating mechanisms outperform binary ones empirically — ReDit provides formal bounds showing optimization time scales inversely with reward variance (Theorem 1), Smooth Operator achieves +5.6% with sigmoid continuous rewards for VLM GRPO (though CRITICALLY requires AP-GRPO to prevent signal dilution under group normalization), and Smooth Gate Functions formalizes four axioms for admissible gate functions. Direction 5: Multi-reward normalization requires special treatment — GDPO (ICML 2026, NVIDIA) proves that directly applying GRPO normalization to aggregated multi-reward combinations causes advantage collapse, and proposes decoupled per-reward normalization that preserves substantially more distinct advantage groups; FGRPO independently finds that decoupled normalization is necessary for multi-reward faithfulness. The crucial synthesis combines three observations: (A) Scientific visual reasoning exhibits an epistemic dependency — visual grounding is a NECESSARY CONDITION for valid reasoning (you cannot produce a correct explanation of a misperceived figure) — creating a natural gating hierarchy validated by From Seeing to Thinking and Bad Seeing or Bad Thinking. (B) Continuous gating is empirically and analytically superior to binary gating, supported by multiple independent results (ReDit, Gradient Starvation, Smooth Operator) and our Proposition 1 (degenerate group elimination), because binary gating produces degenerate zero-gradient groups and discards graded quality signals. Critically, FGRPO's own ablation confirms this: their binary multiplicative gating fails precisely because it MASKS gradient signal. (C) Multi-reward composites require decoupled normalization (GDPO) to prevent advantage collapse — our three-tier gated reward is exactly the setting where this matters most. We present continuous gating superiority as a well-motivated hypothesis — supported by convergent empirical evidence AND our original Proposition 1 — that our ablation suite (A2/A3 comparing continuous vs binary, A10 comparing sigmoid gating vs Lagrangian constraints) will directly validate in the non-verifiable multimodal setting. The sigmoid gating formula g(x)=σ((x−τ)/T) has been applied at inference-time for visual reliability calibration (Grounding the Score) but never integrated into RL training rewards for non-verifiable tasks. Where RaR demonstrates rubric RL for non-verifiable science with flat aggregation, we add hierarchical gating to encode the epistemic dependency. Where Smooth Operator demonstrates continuous sigmoid rewards for verifiable VLM tasks, we extend to non-verifiable scientific reasoning with multi-tier structure. Where GDPO addresses multi-reward advantage collapse via decoupled normalization on flat reward combinations, we combine it with hierarchical gating encoding epistemic dependencies. Additionally, POW3R demonstrates that static rubric weights are suboptimal because criteria saturate or become unreachable at different training stages — motivating policy-aware adaptive gating. And Reward Hacking in Rubric-Based RL reveals systematic exploitation patterns in rubric rewards for scientific/medical domains — motivating our integration of the self-internalization gap as a training diagnostic.",
  "landscape": "PERCEPTION-AWARE RL FOR VLMs: VPPO (arXiv:2510.09285, ICLR 2026) uses Trajectory Advantage Shaping and Token Gradient Filtering based on KL-divergence visual dependency — verifiable tasks only, no explicit gating. VGPO (arXiv:2604.09349, ACL 2026) introduces a binary Visual Gate with attention compensation to counteract temporal visual forgetting — verifiable tasks, binary indicator gate. PAPO (arXiv:2507.06448, ICLR 2026) adds Implicit Perception Loss via masked-image KL divergence and Double Entropy Loss to prevent KL_prcp hacking — verifiable tasks, finds 67% of failures from perception. From Seeing to Thinking (arXiv:2605.20177, ICML 2026) decouples perception and reasoning into staged GRPO training, proving perception-first ordering yields +4.6pp and that 86.9% of errors are perceptual — strongest validation of perception→reasoning dependency but uses hard stage boundaries, verifiable. Bad Seeing or Bad Thinking (arXiv:2605.14054, ICML 2026 Spotlight) introduces MoCA for modality-aware credit assignment via blindfolded reasoning proxy — discrete routing, verifiable. Perceval (arXiv:2604.24583, Apr 2026) integrates perception reward into RL training via claim-level error grounding — extracts image-related claims, verifies each against visual evidence, then applies token-level advantage penalties A'[i,t] := A[i] − α·m[i,t]·|A[i]| on hallucinated spans identified by Perceval within GRPO training; directly relevant to our Tier-1 claim-level decomposition but operates at token-level granularity rather than tier-level gating. PRCO (arXiv:2603.28618) splits VLM into Observer/Solver roles with differentiated rewards — verifiable, dual-role architecture. Perception-R1 (arXiv:2506.07218) adds visual perception reward to RLVR — verifiable. Vision-SR1 (arXiv:2508.19652) decomposes VLM reasoning with self-rewarding — verifiable. ALL of these address verifiable tasks only; our work extends perception-aware gating to non-verifiable settings. MULTI-REWARD NORMALIZATION AND SIGNAL PRESERVATION: GDPO (arXiv:2601.05242, ICML 2026, NVIDIA) identifies that directly applying GRPO to normalize aggregated multi-reward combinations causes them to collapse into identical advantage values. Solution: decoupled per-reward normalization Â_k = (r_k − mean(r_k))/std(r_k) for each reward k independently, then aggregate. Preserves substantially more distinct advantage groups as rollouts/rewards grow. Achieves +2.7% accuracy and +4% format compliance on tool-calling, +6.3% on AIME math reasoning over multi-reward GRPO. Most directly relevant signal preservation mechanism for our three-tier composite reward. Smooth Operator (arXiv:2601.07695) proposes SNRA — a dynamically parameterized sigmoid function transforming numerical errors into continuous rewards for VLM GRPO on verifiable spatial tasks. CRITICAL FINDING: smooth sigmoid rewards under vanilla GRPO's group normalization suffer from advantage collapse because relative normalization washes out fine-grained differences; AP-GRPO (Absolute-Preserving) is required to unlock gains (+5.6% over binary). Verifiable tasks only. CONSTRAINED VS GATED APPROACHES: FGRPO Faithful GRPO (arXiv:2604.08476) enforces visual grounding and logical consistency as CONSTRAINTS via Lagrangian dual ascent: ℒ(θ,λ)=𝔼[R_task]+λ_C(𝔼[R_C]−τ_C)+λ_S(𝔼[R_S]−τ_S)+λ_G(𝔼[R_G]−τ_G), with adaptive multiplier update λ_k ← clip(0, λ_max, λ_k + η·(τ_k − c̄_k)). Reduces inconsistency from 24.5% to 1.7%, improves grounding by +13%. CRITICAL TABLE 2 FINDING: naive binary multiplicative gating R=g(R_ground)·R_task DEGRADES accuracy by −1.7pp while inconsistency remains at 19.6% — because binary masking eliminates gradient signal from gated components. Lagrangian constraints with decoupled normalization outperform both additive and multiplicative alternatives. Our continuous sigmoid gating addresses the binary masking pathology that FGRPO identifies: g(x) ∈ (0,1) never fully masks, preserving gradient signal. Combined with GDPO-style decoupled normalization, our approach avoids both the masking problem and the advantage collapse problem. Verifiable tasks only; we extend to non-verifiable. CONTINUOUS REWARD AND GATING MECHANISMS: Grounding the Score (arXiv:2603.16253) uses α(r)=σ(β(r−τ)) with β=10, τ=0.5 to gate PRM step rewards by visual reliability — INFERENCE-TIME ONLY calibration for best-of-N reranking, no RL training, structurally identical sigmoid formula to our g_k(x). VL-MDR (arXiv:2604.05445) uses visual-aware gating to dynamically select and weight 21 fine-grained reward dimensions — closest architectural analogue at reward modeling level, DPO-based not RL. ReDit (arXiv:2506.18631) adds zero-mean noise to discrete rewards making them continuous; Theorem 1 proves optimization time lower-bounded by inverse of reward variance; Proposition 1: dithered rewards produce unbiased gradients; achieves GRPO-equivalent performance in 10% of steps; +1.5-4.5 points across 6 models. Gradient Starvation in Binary-Reward GRPO (arXiv:2605.07689) shows binary rewards cause 69% degenerate groups at G=4 (zero advantage); Proposition 2 proves D_real ≥ p^G + (1−p)^G by Jensen's inequality. Smooth Gate Functions (arXiv:2602.19345) formalizes four axioms for admissible gate functions (continuous differentiability, on-policy maximum, monotonic attenuation, outlier suppression); smooth gates acquire format 4× faster and prevent entropy decay. PEPO (arXiv:2603.22847) uses smooth gating for multimodal token-level advantage estimation. VERIFIABLE MULTIMODAL + GATED/STRUCTURED REWARDS: PaLMR (arXiv:2603.06652) uses gated hierarchical reward R = S_vis·(α·S_ans + (1−α)·S_fmt) where BINARY visual fidelity gates answer reward — closest gating principle but verifiable with binary gate. SR-MCR (arXiv:2512.22545) integrates five sub-rewards with GRPO — flat combination, verifiable. RuCL (arXiv:2602.21628) stratified rubric-based curriculum — verifiable. PEARL (CVPR 2026) binary perception-reasoning gate. CogFlow (ICLR 2026) Visual-Gated Policy Optimization — binary gate. Vero (arXiv:2604.04917) task-routed rewards — verifiable. V-Triune (arXiv:2505.18129) sample-level reward routing — verifiable. NON-VERIFIABLE RUBRIC-BASED RL: RaR 'Rubrics as Rewards' (arXiv:2507.17746, ICLR 2026, Scale AI) — PUBLISHED ICLR 2026 paper doing rubric-based RL (GRPO) for non-verifiable science/medicine. Uses instance-specific rubrics with Essential/Important/Optional/Pitfall weighting. Implicit aggregation outperforms explicit per-criterion evaluation. Up to 31% improvement on HealthBench. NO gating mechanism — flat weighted aggregation. Most directly relevant published work; we extend with hierarchical gating + multimodal scientific figure reasoning. DRO (arXiv:2506.13351) BINARY rubric-gating as hard feasibility constraints — text-only. Training AI Co-Scientists (arXiv:2512.23707) rubric RL for scientific plan generation — text-only. Rubric-ARM (arXiv:2602.01511) — text-only. Writing-Zero (arXiv:2506.00103) pairwise GenRM — text-only. Rubric-Grounded RL (arXiv:2605.08061) — text-only. RubricEM (arXiv:2605.10899) — text-only. ARES (arXiv:2605.23454) automated rubric synthesis at scale — text-only. AutoRubric-R1V (arXiv:2510.14738) auto-constructs rubrics for multimodal reasoning with self-aggregation and dual reward integration. NON-VERIFIABLE MULTIMODAL: RubiCap (arXiv:2603.09160) rubric-based RL for dense captioning — no gating. ClaimDiff-RL (arXiv:2605.20278) claim-level decomposition with graded severity. rDPO (arXiv:2604.13029) rubrics for multimodal DPO — DPO not RL. REWARD DYNAMICS: Reward Hacking in Rubric-Based RL (arXiv:2605.12474) three exploitation patterns; self-internalization gap (r=0.91-0.97). POW3R (arXiv:2605.20164) policy-aware rubric weighting outperforms static. Reward Design for Physical Reasoning (arXiv:2604.13993) accuracy > flat rubric on verifiable, but rubric improves reasoning quality. GRADIENT THEORY: Razin et al. (arXiv:2310.20703, ICLR 2024) prove that RL finetuning gradients vanish when reward standard deviation under the model is small, due to the interaction between the reward objective and the softmax operator — motivating reward designs that maximize within-group variance, which continuous gated rewards naturally provide. GR3 (arXiv:2603.10535) addresses length inflation via multiplicative rescaling; Appendix A notes multiplicative shaping subsumes heuristic binary gating in binary-reward settings — concerns length control, not hierarchical quality gating. THE GAP: No work combines (1) continuous hierarchical gating in RL training (sigmoid gating exists only at inference-time in Grounding the Score and for verifiable VLM tasks in Smooth Operator; all RL training gating is binary or discrete Lagrangian) with (2) decoupled per-tier normalization preventing multi-reward advantage collapse (GDPO addresses flat multi-reward, not hierarchically gated) with (3) non-verifiable rubric-based RL (RaR does rubric RL for non-verifiable science but with flat aggregation, no gating) with (4) multimodal scientific reasoning requiring perception→reasoning dependency (validated by From Seeing to Thinking, Bad Seeing or Bad Thinking, PAPO, Perceval, but only exploited in verifiable settings) with (5) policy-aware adaptive weight/threshold scheduling with signal preservation.",
  "inspired_by": "Synthesis of convergent empirical evidence across five established directions. RaR (ICLR 2026) demonstrates rubric-based GRPO works for non-verifiable science but uses flat aggregation without gating — we add hierarchical structure encoding the perception→reasoning epistemic dependency. From Seeing to Thinking (ICML 2026) proves perception is a prerequisite scaffold (86.9% of errors are perceptual) but uses hard stage boundaries on verifiable tasks — we implement this dependency as continuous gates within a unified RL objective for non-verifiable tasks. Smooth Operator demonstrates sigmoid continuous rewards improve VLM GRPO on verifiable tasks but requires AP-GRPO to prevent signal dilution — we extend to non-verifiable scientific reasoning and incorporate GDPO-style decoupled normalization (more principled for multi-reward settings). GDPO (ICML 2026) proves multi-reward GRPO normalization causes advantage collapse and proposes decoupled normalization — our three-tier gated composite is exactly the multi-reward setting where this is needed. FGRPO demonstrates Lagrangian dual ascent for visual grounding constraints but reveals binary multiplicative gating degrades performance (−1.7pp accuracy) — our continuous sigmoid gating + GDPO decoupled normalization avoids both the binary masking pathology and the advantage collapse pathology. Grounding the Score uses the identical sigmoid formula α(r)=σ(β(r−τ)) for inference-time visual reliability gating — we deploy the same functional form within the RL training loop where it shapes gradient dynamics. Perceval demonstrates claim-level perception verification integrated into GRPO via token-level advantage modulation — directly informs our Tier-1 claim-level decomposition approach. Multiple empirical results converge to support continuous > binary: ReDit (Theorem 1: optimization time ∝ 1/reward_variance; 10× convergence speedup), Gradient Starvation (69% degenerate groups with binary rewards), Smooth Gate Functions (4 axioms for admissible gates). Additionally, we contribute Proposition 1 (Degenerate Group Elimination): continuous gating provably eliminates gate-induced degenerate groups that binary gating cannot avoid. POW3R informs policy-aware adaptation. Reward Hacking in Rubric-Based RL informs anti-exploitation monitoring.",
  "approach": "We propose GatedRubric-GRPO, which introduces CONTINUOUS hierarchical gating with DECOUPLED NORMALIZATION for non-verifiable multimodal scientific reasoning within GRPO training on Qwen3-VL-8B. The key technical innovations over existing approaches: (a) vs RaR (ICLR 2026): adds hierarchical gating encoding perception→reasoning dependency to flat rubric aggregation; (b) vs DRO: generalizes from binary to continuous gating and from text to multimodal; (c) vs PaLMR: generalizes from binary to continuous gating and from verifiable to non-verifiable; (d) vs Smooth Operator: extends continuous sigmoid rewards from verifiable to non-verifiable tasks with multi-tier hierarchical structure, and replaces AP-GRPO with GDPO-style decoupled normalization for multi-reward signal preservation; (e) vs Grounding the Score: deploys the sigmoid gating formula within RL training (affecting gradient dynamics and policy optimization) rather than inference-time calibration; (f) vs GDPO: adds hierarchical gating encoding epistemic dependencies atop decoupled normalization (GDPO normalizes flat reward combinations without structural dependencies); (g) vs FGRPO: continuous sigmoid gating instead of binary Lagrangian constraints, applied to non-verifiable tasks — FGRPO's own Table 2 shows binary multiplicative gating degrades accuracy by −1.7pp, motivating our continuous alternative; (h) vs Perceval: tier-level gating hierarchy instead of token-level advantage penalties, applied to non-verifiable scientific reasoning.\n\nORIGINAL ANALYTICAL CONTRIBUTION — PROPOSITION 1 (Degenerate Group Elimination): Consider a GRPO group of G i.i.d. rollouts with gated reward g(R₁)·R₂ where R₁ is the gating score.\n\n(a) Under binary gating g_b(x) = 𝟙(x ≥ τ) with P(R₁ ≥ τ) = p: The probability that all gate values in a group are identical (producing zero gate-induced advantage variance) is P_degen = p^G + (1−p)^G ≥ 2^{1−G} (by Jensen's inequality, recovering Gradient Starvation's bound). At G=4, p=0.5: P_degen = 0.125. At realistic p ∈ [0.3, 0.7]: P_degen ∈ [0.13, 0.25].\n\n(b) Under continuous sigmoid gating g_c(x) = σ((x−τ)/T) with T > 0, when R₁ has a continuous distribution (density f): P(all gate values identical) = 0. Continuous gating PROVABLY ELIMINATES gate-induced degenerate groups.\n\n(c) The expected within-group gate variance satisfies: E[Var_G(g_c(R₁⁽ⁱ⁾))] = ((G−1)/G) · Var(g_c(R₁)) > 0 for all T > 0 when R₁ has non-degenerate support spanning τ. Under binary gating: E[Var_G(g_b(R₁⁽ⁱ⁾))] < ((G−1)/G) · p(1−p), because degenerate groups contribute zero gate variance.\n\n(d) There exists a finite T* > 0 maximizing E[Var_G(g_c(R₁⁽ⁱ⁾))], and at this optimum the continuous gate achieves STRICTLY HIGHER expected within-group gate variance than the binary gate. Proof sketch: As T → 0, g_c → g_b, recovering the binary variance. As T increases from 0, gate values spread from {0,1} to nearby continuous values — within non-degenerate groups this reduces per-sample variance slightly, but degenerate groups (which contributed ZERO variance under binary gating) now contribute POSITIVE variance. The net effect is positive for small T > 0 by a dominated convergence argument on the degenerate group measure. As T → ∞, all gate values converge to 0.5, and Var → 0.\n\nThis is a modest but original analytical result that directly motivates continuous gating in GRPO training beyond citing others' empirical findings. Combined with ReDit's Theorem 1 (optimization time ∝ 1/reward_variance) and Razin et al.'s vanishing gradient result, higher within-group variance translates to stronger gradient signal and faster convergence.\n\nCONTINUOUS GATING FORMULATION: The composite reward decomposes into three epistemically dependent tiers:\n\nR = w₁·R₁ + w₂·g₁(R₁)·R₂ + w₃·g₁(R₁)·g₂(R₂)·R₃\n\nwhere g_k(x) = σ((x − τ_k) / T_k) are sigmoid gate functions with temperature T_k controlling sharpness. Key properties: (1) As T_k → 0, g_k → binary indicator 𝟙(x ≥ τ_k), recovering DRO/PaLMR-style hard gating — our formulation subsumes binary gating as a limiting case. (2) For finite T_k, g_k is continuously differentiable, producing non-zero gradients at all reward values. (3) CRITICALLY, the additive base term w₁·R₁ ALWAYS provides gradient for perception quality — even when gates attenuate Tier-2/3, unlike FGRPO's multiplicative gating where R=g(R_ground)·R_task zeros ALL gradient when g=0. (4) T_k can be scheduled during training (warm→cool), implementing an explicit curriculum from exploration to exploitation.\n\nDECOUPLED NORMALIZATION (addressing GDPO's and Smooth Operator's findings): GDPO (ICML 2026) demonstrates that aggregating multiple rewards before GRPO normalization collapses distinct reward combinations into identical advantages (+6.3% improvement from decoupling on AIME). This applies directly to our three-tier composite: normalizing R = w₁·R₁ + w₂·g₁·R₂ + w₃·g₁·g₂·R₃ as a single scalar would collapse information about which tier drives quality differences. Our signal preservation strategy: (a) PRIMARY: GDPO-style decoupled per-tier normalization — each tier reward R_k is independently group-normalized before gated aggregation: Â_k = (R_k − mean(R_k))/std(R_k), then A_total = w₁·Â₁ + w₂·g₁·Â₂ + w₃·g₁·g₂·Â₃ with batch normalization. This preserves per-tier signal discriminability. (b) ALTERNATIVE (ablated): AP-GRPO-inspired absolute preservation following Smooth Operator. (c) Smooth Operator's specific concern — that continuous rewards under vanilla GRPO normalization suffer advantage collapse — is further mitigated in our setting because decoupled normalization operates per-tier rather than on the composite, and our base rewards are already continuous LLM-judge scores (unlike Smooth Operator which transforms binary→continuous). We ablate normalization strategy explicitly (A9 vs A11).\n\nLAGRANGIAN VS SIGMOID GATING (addressing FGRPO): FGRPO proposes Lagrangian dual ascent as an alternative to gating for encoding the perception→reasoning dependency: ℒ(θ,λ)=𝔼[R_task]+Σ_k λ_k(𝔼[R_k]−τ_k), with adaptive λ updates. Compared to our sigmoid gating: (1) FGRPO's Lagrangian treats perception as a CONSTRAINT (R_grounding ≥ τ) satisfied or violated, while our sigmoid gating treats it as a CONTINUOUS MODULATOR of downstream reward. In non-verifiable settings where grounding quality is inherently graded (a figure can be 70% correctly perceived), continuous modulation is more natural than threshold constraints. (2) FGRPO's dual ascent adaptively reweights constraint importance during training, which our POW3R-inspired adaptive variant also achieves for gate temperatures and tier weights. (3) FGRPO operates on verifiable tasks with binary accuracy and binary consistency rewards; our non-verifiable setting has continuous base rewards throughout. (4) We add FGRPO-style Lagrangian constraint as ablation A10 to directly compare the two mechanisms.\n\nTIER-1 (Visual Grounding, continuous 0-1): Inspired by Perceval's claim-level error grounding and ClaimDiff-RL's claim-level decomposition, we decompose model outputs into atomic visual claims and verify each against the figure. Where Perceval applies token-level advantage penalties (A'[i,t] := A[i] − α·m[i,t]·|A[i]|) for fine-grained supervision within each response, our Tier-1 score aggregates claim verification into a continuous sequence-level grounding score that serves as a hierarchical gate for downstream tiers. The two approaches are complementary: Perceval modulates WITHIN-response credit assignment, while our gating modulates ACROSS-tier reward structure. Programmatic checks (element identification, data reading, spatial description) combined with lightweight LLM verification produce a continuous grounding score.\n\nTIER-2 (Structural Quality, continuously gated on Tier-1): A frozen LLM judge (Qwen3-32B) evaluates logical coherence, evidence-claim alignment, domain terminology, and visual-textual consistency using discipline-specific rubric templates following RaR's rubric design principles (self-contained criteria, expert grounding, importance weighting with Essential/Important/Optional/Pitfall categories following Dr.SCI). Rubric templates auto-generated following ARES's pipeline, then expert-calibrated. Continuously gated by g₁(R₁): when visual grounding is poor, structural quality reward is smoothly attenuated (NOT zeroed as in binary gating), providing gradient signal proportional to grounding quality.\n\nTIER-3 (Reasoning Quality, continuously gated on Tier-1 AND Tier-2): Bootstrapped pairwise comparison within GRPO rollout groups assesses analytical depth, interpretive insight, explanation completeness — extending Writing-Zero's BRPO to multimodal. Continuously gated by g₁(R₁)·g₂(R₂).\n\nPOLICY-AWARE ADAPTIVE VARIANT (GatedRubric-GRPO+): Inspired by POW3R's finding that static rubric weights are suboptimal and FGRPO's adaptive Lagrange multipliers, we implement an adaptive variant where: (a) per-criterion contrastiveness is computed from rollout variance within each GRPO group, (b) weights w₁, w₂, w₃ and temperatures T₁, T₂ are rescaled based on criterion contrastiveness with EMA smoothing, (c) category-level normalization preserves the tier structure, and (d) GDPO-style decoupled normalization prevents signal dilution.\n\nANTI-HACKING MONITORING: Integrating the self-internalization gap from Reward Hacking in Rubric-Based RL, we compute the divergence between the policy's prompt-only distribution and rubric-conditioned distribution using only policy log-probabilities. This provides a verifier-free early-stopping diagnostic (r=0.91-0.97 correlation with reference panel).\n\nTRAINING TASKS (genuinely non-verifiable):\n\n(1) Scientific figure explanation generation using MMSci (Nature Communications figures, 72 disciplines) — 10K stratified sample across 18 discipline groups. RE-ANNOTATION PIPELINE: Reference captions decomposed into atomic claims by Qwen3-32B, converted to per-figure rubric criteria across 7 dimensions: Visual Accuracy, Sub-figure Coverage, Quantitative Fidelity, Scientific Terminology, Methodological Context, Interpretive Validity, Structural Description. Each criterion assigned severity following RaR's Essential/Important/Optional/Pitfall categorization. Teacher committee of 3 VLMs generates alternative captions for consensus extraction. MOTIVATION: CIDEr scores are 0.00-3.73 across ALL models on MMSci, demonstrating reference-based metrics are fundamentally inadequate.\n\n(2) Open-ended scientific graph analysis using SciGraphQA re-annotated with rubric scoring.\n\n(3) SciCritique-5K: A new benchmark of ~5K scientific figure critique examples. CONSTRUCTION PIPELINE: (a) Source: ArXiv papers (2020-2025) across 5 STEM domains. (b) Figure type classification using SigLIP visual encoder. (c) Critique generation: 3-model ensemble. (d) Rubric dimensions (8). (e) Each dimension: 5-point ordinal scale + Essential/Important/Optional/Pitfall classification (Dr.SCI approach, also used by RaR). (f) LLM annotation with 3-run median voting. (g) Expert validation on 20% subset (1K items) using LLM-ASSISTED REVIEW PIPELINE: LLM generates initial rubric annotations, domain experts review and correct (reducing per-item time from ~25 min unaided to ~8 min review), 3 annotators per item, target Krippendorff's α ≥ 0.75.\n\nCONTROLLED COMPARISON: CharXiv and SciFIBench as verifiable baselines.\n\nCOMPREHENSIVE ABLATION SUITE (11 conditions):\n(A1) Flat composite: R = w₁·R₁ + w₂·R₂ + w₃·R₃ (no gating — RaR-style)\n(A2) DRO-style binary rubric-gating: hard accept/reject at rollout-group level\n(A3) PaLMR-style binary visual gate: R₁ binarized, indicator function gates\n(A4) POW3R-style policy-aware weighting WITHOUT gating: adaptive weights but flat combination\n(A5) Dynamic weighting à la RuCL: rubric weights adjust during training but without gating\n(A6) Tier-1+2 only (no reasoning quality tier)\n(A7) Tier-1+3 only (no structural quality tier)\n(A8) Grounding-the-Score-style inference-time gating: train with flat rewards, apply sigmoid gating at inference for best-of-N selection — tests whether training-time gating provides value beyond inference-time reranking\n(A9) GatedRubric-GRPO with AP-GRPO instead (1) STRENGTHEN ANALYTICAL CONTRIBUTION: Proposition 1 part (d) claims existence of optimal T* but the proof sketch is informal. Consider formalizing it: under standard distributional assumptions (e.g., R₁ ~ Beta(α,β) or Gaussian), derive the optimal T* in closed form and compute the variance ratio V_continuous(T*)/V_binary. This would transform a modest observation into a concrete, citable theoretical result.

(2) ADD PRELIMINARY EXPERIMENT: Even a small-scale experiment (e.g., 100 training steps on 1K MMSci subset) comparing continuous vs binary gating on actual GRPO rollout statistics would dramatically strengthen the paper. (5) MAKE THE VARIANCE-CONVERGENCE CHAIN EXPLICIT: The argument 'continuous gating → higher gate variance (Prop 1) → higher reward variance → faster convergence (ReDit Thm 1)' requires stating how gate variance translates to composite reward variance.   "title": "GatedRubric-GRPO: Continuous Hierarchical Gating with Decoupled Normalization for Non-Verifiable Multimodal Scientific Reasoning",
  "core_problem": "Reinforcement learning with structured rewards has advanced rapidly across three converging axes: (1) gated/hierarchical rewards for verifiable multimodal tasks (PaLMR, PEARL, CogFlow use binary visual gates; VGPO uses a binary Visual Gate for attention compensation), (2) rubric-based RL for non-verifiable tasks (RaR [ICLR 2026] uses rubric rewards with GRPO for medicine/science; DRO uses binary rubric-gates as feasibility constraints; Training AI Co-Scientists applies rubric RL to scientific plan generation), and (3) perception-aware VLM training (VPPO, PAPO, From Seeing to Thinking [ICML 2026] demonstrate perception-first training is critical; Bad Seeing or Bad Thinking [ICML 2026] introduces MoCA for perception-reasoning credit assignment; Perceval integrates claim-level perception verification into RL training via token-level advantage modulation). However, ALL existing gating mechanisms in RL training — whether for visual fidelity (PaLMR), rubric feasibility (DRO), essential criteria qualification (rDPO), visual attention compensation (VGPO), or Lagrangian visual grounding constraints (FGRPO) — employ BINARY or DISCRETE constraint mechanisms: hard accept/reject, pass/fail, or threshold-based Lagrangian penalties. Separately, works exploring continuous alternatives to binary rewards have shown strong empirical benefits: ReDit demonstrates 10× faster convergence when adding noise to make discrete rewards continuous (with formal optimization time bounds in Theorem 1); Gradient Starvation in Binary-Reward GRPO shows 69% of GRPO groups become degenerate (zero-advantage) with binary rewards at group size 4; and Smooth Operator demonstrates that sigmoid-shaped continuous rewards improve VLM GRPO by +5.6% over binary baselines when combined with absolute-preserving advantage estimation (AP-GRPO). Furthermore, GDPO (ICML 2026) proves that naive GRPO normalization of multi-reward aggregation causes distinct reward combinations to collapse into identical advantage values — directly relevant when composite rewards combine multiple gated tiers. Meanwhile, Grounding the Score uses the sigmoid formula α(r)=σ(β(r−τ)) for inference-time calibration of visual reliability in process reward models — the same functional form we propose for RL training. The problem is especially acute for non-verifiable scientific visual reasoning — tasks like scientific figure explanation, graph-based analytical interpretation, and figure critique — where both visual grounding quality and reasoning quality are INHERENTLY CONTINUOUS and GRADED. A figure can be 70% correctly perceived; a scientific explanation can be partially valid. Binary gating and discrete constraint mechanisms discard this graded signal.",
  "opportunity": "The landscape reveals a specific technical gap at the intersection of five established directions, each now well-validated independently. Direction 1: Gated multimodal rewards exist (PaLMR, PEARL, CogFlow, VGPO) but use binary gates on verifiable tasks. FGRPO uses Lagrangian dual ascent for visual grounding constraints — a principled alternative to gating — but its Table 2 reveals that naive binary multiplicative gating DEGRADES accuracy by −1.7pp while inconsistency remains at 19.6%, because binary masking eliminates gradient signal from gated components. Direction 2: Rubric-based non-verifiable RL is now established — RaR (ICLR 2026) demonstrates up to 31% improvement on medical reasoning with rubric rewards via GRPO, but uses flat weighted aggregation without gating or hierarchical structure. DRO uses binary rubric-gates but is text-only. Direction 3: Perception-aware VLM training is validated — From Seeing to Thinking (ICML 2026) proves that 86.9% of VLM errors stem from perception failures and that perception-first staged training yields +4.6pp improvement; Bad Seeing or Bad Thinking (ICML 2026) shows MoCA credit assignment between perception and reasoning; PAPO finds 67% of failures from perception errors; Perceval demonstrates claim-level error grounding with token-level RL integration for perception. Direction 4: Continuous rewards/gating mechanisms outperform binary ones empirically — ReDit provides formal bounds showing optimization time scales inversely with reward variance (Theorem 1), Smooth Operator achieves +5.6% with sigmoid continuous rewards for VLM GRPO (though CRITICALLY requires AP-GRPO to prevent signal dilution under group normalization), and Smooth Gate Functions formalizes four axioms for admissible gate functions.   "approach": "We propose GatedRubric-GRPO, which introduces CONTINUOUS hierarchical gating with DECOUPLED NORMALIZATION for non-verifiable multimodal scientific reasoning within GRPO training on Qwen3-VL-8B. The key technical innovations over existing approaches: (a) vs RaR (ICLR 2026): adds hierarchical gating encoding perception→reasoning dependency to flat rubric aggregation; (b) vs DRO: generalizes from binary to continuous gating and from text to multimodal; (c) vs PaLMR: generalizes from binary to continuous gating and from verifiable to non-verifiable; (d) vs Smooth Operator: extends continuous sigmoid rewards from verifiable to non-verifiable tasks with multi-tier hierarchical structure, and replaces AP-GRPO with GDPO-style decoupled normalization for multi-reward signal preservation; (e) vs Grounding the Score: deploys the sigmoid gating formula within RL training (affecting gradient dynamics and policy optimization) rather than inference-time calibration; (f) vs GDPO: adds hierarchical gating encoding epistemic dependencies atop decoupled normalization (GDPO normalizes flat reward combinations without structural dependencies); (g) vs FGRPO: continuous sigmoid gating instead of binary Lagrangian constraints, applied to non-verifiable tasks — FGRPO's own Table 2 shows binary multiplicative gating degrades accuracy by −1.7pp, motivating our continuous alternative; (h) vs Perceval: tier-level gating hierarchy instead of token-level advantage penalties, applied to non-verifiable scientific reasoning.\n\nORIGINAL ANALYTICAL CONTRIBUTION — PROPOSITION 1 (Degenerate Group Elimination): Consider a GRPO group of G i.i.d. rollouts with gated reward g(R₁)·R₂ where R₁ is the gating score.\n\n(a) Under binary gating g_b(x) = 𝟙(x ≥ τ) with P(R₁ ≥ τ) = p: The probability that all gate values in a group are identical (producing zero gate-induced advantage variance) is P_degen = p^G + (1−p)^G ≥ 2^{1−G} (by Jensen's inequality, recovering Gradient Starvation's bound). At G=4, p=0.5: P_degen = 0.125. At realistic p ∈ [0.3, 0.7]: P_degen ∈ [0.13, 0.25].\n\n(b) Under continuous sigmoid gating g_c(x) = σ((x−τ)/T) with T > 0, when R₁ has a continuous distribution (density f): P(all gate values identical) = 0. Continuous gating PROVABLY ELIMINATES gate-induced degenerate groups.\n\n(c) The expected within-group gate variance satisfies: E[Var_G(g_c(R₁⁽ⁱ⁾))] = ((G−1)/G) · Var(g_c(R₁)) > 0 for all T > 0 when R₁ has non-degenerate support spanning τ. Under binary gating: E[Var_G(g_b(R₁⁽ⁱ⁾))] < ((G−1)/G) · p(1−p), because degenerate groups contribute zero gate variance.\n\n(d) There exists a finite T* > 0 maximizing E[Var_G(g_c(R₁⁽ⁱ⁾))], and at this optimum the continuous gate achieves STRICTLY HIGHER expected within-group gate variance than the binary gate. Proof sketch: As T → 0, g_c → g_b, recovering the binary variance. As T increases from 0, gate values spread from {0,1} to nearby continuous values — within non-degenerate groups this reduces per-sample variance slightly, but degenerate groups (which contributed ZERO variance under binary gating) now contribute POSITIVE variance. The net effect is positive for small T > 0 by a dominated convergence argument on the degenerate group measure. As T → ∞, all gate values converge to 0.5, and Var → 0.\n\nThis is a modest but original analytical result that directly motivates continuous gating in GRPO training beyond citing others' empirical findings. Combined with ReDit's Theorem 1 (optimization time ∝ 1/reward_variance) and Razin et al.'s vanishing gradient result, higher within-group variance translates to stronger gradient signal and faster convergence.\n\nCONTINUOUS GATING FORMULATION: The composite reward decomposes into three epistemically dependent tiers:\n\nR = w₁·R₁ + w₂·g₁(R₁)·R₂ + w₃·g₁(R₁)·g₂(R₂)·R₃\n\nwhere g_k(x) = σ((x − τ_k) / T_k) are sigmoid gate functions with temperature T_k controlling sharpness. Key properties: (1) As T_k → 0, g_k → binary indicator 𝟙(x ≥ τ_k), recovering DRO/PaLMR-style hard gating — our formulation subsumes binary gating as a limiting case. (2) For finite T_k, g_k is continuously differentiable, producing non-zero gradients at all reward values. (3) CRITICALLY, the additive base term w₁·R₁ ALWAYS provides gradient for perception quality — even when gates attenuate Tier-2/3, unlike FGRPO's multiplicative gating where R=g(R_ground)·R_task zeros ALL gradient when g=0. (4) T_k can be scheduled during training (warm→cool), implementing an explicit curriculum from exploration to exploitation.\n\nDECOUPLED NORMALIZATION (addressing GDPO's and Smooth Operator's findings): GDPO (ICML 2026) demonstrates that aggregating multiple rewards before GRPO normalization collapses distinct reward combinations into identical advantages (+6.3% improvement from decoupling on AIME). This applies directly to our three-tier composite: normalizing R = w₁·R₁ + w₂·g₁·R₂ + w₃·g₁·g₂·R₃ as a single scalar would collapse information about which tier drives quality differences. Our signal preservation strategy: (a) PRIMARY: GDPO-style decoupled per-tier normalization — each tier reward R_k is independently group-normalized before gated aggregation: Â_k = (R_k − mean(R_k))/std(R_k), then A_total = w₁·Â₁ + w₂·g₁·Â₂ + w₃·g₁·g₂·Â₃ with batch normalization. This preserves per-tier signal discriminability. (b) ALTERNATIVE (ablated): AP-GRPO-inspired absolute preservation following Smooth Operator. (c) Smooth Operator's specific concern — that continuous rewards under vanilla GRPO normalization suffer advantage collapse — is further mitigated in our setting because decoupled normalization operates per-tier rather than on the composite, and our base rewards are already continuous LLM-judge scores (unlike Smooth Operator which transforms binary→continuous). (4) We add FGRPO-style Lagrangian constraint as ablation A10 to directly compare the two mechanisms.\n\nTIER-1 (Visual Grounding, continuous 0-1): Inspired by Perceval's claim-level error grounding and ClaimDiff-RL's claim-level decomposition, we decompose model outputs into atomic visual claims and verify each against the figure. # PGPO Paper Summary

**Full Title:** "Not All Tokens See Equally: Perception-Grounded Policy Optimization for Large Vision-Language Models"

**Authors:** Zekai Ye, Qiming Li, Xiaocheng Feng, Ruihan Chen, Ziming Li, Haoyu Ren, Kun Chen, Dandan Tu, Bing Qin

## Key Method: PGPO

**Perception-Aware Mechanism:**
The paper introduces "Token Visual Dependency," which measures "the causal information gain of visual inputs via the Kullback-Leibler divergence between visual-conditioned and text-only predictive distributions." This enables fine-grained credit assignment.

**Advantage Reshaping:**
PGPO employs "a threshold-gated, mass-conserving mechanism" that "actively amplifies learning signals for visually-dependent tokens while suppressing gradient noise from linguistic priors." Rather than distributing identical advantages across all tokens, it dynamically reshapes token-level advantages based on visual dependency strength.

## Main Contributions

The framework addresses a critical flaw in existing RLVR (Reinforcement Learning from Verifiable Rewards) methods by recognizing that visual dependency is "highly sparse and semantically pivotal," enabling more effective multimodal reasoning optimization.

## Results & Benchmarks

- **Improvement:** 18.7% average boost across seven challenging multimodal reasoning benchmarks
- **Model Tested:** Qwen2.5-VL series
- **Task Type:** Verifiable rewards (RLVR framework)
- **Additional Benefits:** Reduces gradient variance, prevents training collapse, and acts as a regularizer

# Research Paper Summary

**Full Title:** "Addressing Overthinking in Large Vision-Language Models via Gated Perception-Reasoning Optimization"

**Authors:** Xingjian Diao, Zheyuan Liu, Chunhui Zhang, Weiyi Wu, Keyi Kong, Lin Shi, Kaize Ding, Soroush Vosoughi, Jiang Gui

---

## Key Method: GPRO

**Gated Perception-Reasoning Optimization** functions as "a meta-reasoning controller that dynamically routes computation among three decision paths" at each generation step:

1. **Lightweight fast path** – direct response generation
2. **Slow perception path** – re-examines visual inputs for improved grounding
3. **Slow reasoning path** – internal self-reflection and deliberation

---

## Core Insight

The paper argues that "reasoning errors often originate from imperfect perception rather than insufficient deliberation," addressing a fundamental visual grounding bottleneck overlooked by prior adaptive reasoning strategies.

---

## Training Approach

The controller learns through:
- **Supervision data:** ~790k samples with failure attribution labels distinguishing perceptual hallucinations from reasoning errors
- **Optimization:** Multi-objective reinforcement learning balancing accuracy and computational efficiency

---

## Results

GPRO demonstrates improvements across five benchmarks, achieving better accuracy and efficiency while producing "significantly shorter responses" compared to existing slow-thinking methods.

---

## Task Type

The paper addresses both verifiable and non-verifiable visual reasoning tasks requiring accurate perception-grounded decision-making.

# Auto-Rubric as Reward: Research Summary

**Full Title:**
"Auto-Rubric as Reward: From Implicit Preferences to Explicit Multimodal Generative Criteria"

**Authors:**
Juanxi Tian, Fengyuan Liu, Jiaming Han, Yilei Jiang, Yongliang Wu, Yesheng Liu, Haodong Li, Furong Xu, Wanhua Li

**Key Methods:**
- Auto-Rubric as Reward (ARR)
- Rubric Policy Optimization (RPO)

**Main Contributions:**

The framework converts implicit preference knowledge into explicit, verifiable quality dimensions. ARR "externalizes a VLM's internalized preference knowledge as prompt-specific rubrics" before pairwise comparisons, reducing evaluation biases. RPO then distills these structured evaluations into robust binary rewards for policy training, replacing opaque scalar regression with structured preference decisions.

**Application to Multimodal Tasks:**

ARR addresses the compositional, multi-dimensional nature of human judgment in multimodal systems. Rather than collapsing preferences into scalar labels, it maintains structured criteria for improved alignment.

**Tasks Evaluated:**
- Text-to-image generation
- Image editing

**Results:**

ARR-RPO outperformed pairwise reward models and VLM judges on these benchmarks, demonstrating that "explicitly externalizing implicit preference knowledge into structured rubrics achieves more reliable, data-efficient multimodal alignment."

**Non-Verifiable Tasks:**

The paper positions rubrics as an alternative to opaque parametric proxies, addressing vulnerability to reward hacking through interpretable constraints rather than tackling inherent task verifiability.

## Key Findings

**GRPO Overview:**
GRPO is a simplified variant of PPO that groups multiple completions per prompt and normalizes rewards within the group to compute advantages, removing the need for a value function.

**Addressing Reward Variance:**
Group-based normalization is especially effective in tasks subject to high variance in difficulty, where single-sample policy gradients either reinforce uninformative components or yield vanishing gradients.

**Theoretical Advances (2026):**
Recent theory repositions the GRPO gradient estimator as a U-statistic: the group-relative gradient is exactly a second-order U-statistic. Additionally, GRPO enjoys a strictly improved convergence rate over unnormalized REINFORCE, with gains characterized by the average within-prompt reward standard deviation across prompts and iterations.

**Training Dynamics:**
Analysis on GSM8K and MATH benchmarks reveals three distinct training phases governed by the interplay between feature orthogonality and reward variance: an early acceleration phase where high variance and orthogonality favor adaptive scaling, a relatively stable transition phase, and a late-stage regime where the loss of orthogonality limits further gains.

**Multi-Objective Extensions:**
Recent work addresses signal degradation in multi-reward settings. GDPO decouples the normalization process by normalizing each reward signal independently within the group before aggregation, instead of summing rewards before normalization.

# Key Findings on GRPO Normalization

## Core Mechanism
The paper reveals that "standard deviation normalization implements an adaptive gradient" in GRPO, addressing a previously unclear aspect of why this technique improves performance in reinforcement learning for language models.

## Reward Variance and Convergence
A formal convergence result is presented: GRPO achieves "strictly improved convergence rate over unnormalized REINFORCE, with gains characterized by the average within-prompt reward standard deviation across prompts and iterations." This directly connects reward variance magnitude to optimization speed.

## Three Training Phases
The research identifies distinct phases where variance effects differ:

1. **Early acceleration**: High variance and orthogonal features enable effective adaptive scaling
2. **Stable transition**: Moderate conditions maintain progress
3. **Late-stage decline**: Loss of feature orthogonality reduces normalization benefits

## Gradient Quality Impact
Within-group reward variance directly influences gradient signal quality through the local curvature lens—higher variance enables stronger adaptive scaling effects during earlier training phases when feature orthogonality remains high. However, this advantage diminishes as orthogonality degrades, suggesting variance alone cannot sustain improvements throughout training.

## Overview

PGPO is a novel fine-grained credit assignment framework designed to address issues with Reinforcement Learning from Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) in Large Vision-Language Models, which suffer from distributing identical advantages across all generated tokens.

## Key Methodology

PGPO uses a threshold-gated, mass-conserving mechanism that amplifies learning signals for visually-dependent tokens while suppressing gradient noise from linguistic priors. The framework quantifies token visual dependency through the Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence between visual-conditioned and text-only predictive distributions.

## Benchmark Results

Extensive experiments based on the Qwen2.5-VL series across seven challenging multimodal reasoning benchmarks demonstrate that PGPO boosts models by 18.7% on average.

## Benefits

Both theoretical and empirical analyses confirm that PGPO effectively reduces gradient variance, prevents training collapse, and acts as a potent regularizer for robust, perception-grounded multimodal reasoning.

Based on the search results, here are the key findings about GPRO (Gated Perception-Reasoning Optimization):

## Overview
GPRO is a meta-reasoning controller that dynamically routes computation among three decision paths at each generation step: a lightweight fast path, a slow perception path for re-examining visual inputs, and a slow reasoning path for internal self-reflection.

## Benchmark Results and Improvements
Experiments on five benchmarks demonstrate that GPRO substantially improves both accuracy and efficiency, outperforming recent slow-thinking methods while generating significantly shorter responses.

## Training Approach
The approach derives large-scale failure attribution supervision from approximately 790k samples, using teacher models to distinguish perceptual hallucinations from reasoning errors. The controller is trained with multi-objective reinforcement learning to optimize the trade-off between task accuracy and computational cost.

## Core Innovation
The work argues that stable reasoning critically depends on low-level visual grounding, and that reasoning errors often originate from imperfect perception rather than insufficient deliberation.

The paper (arXiv 2601.04442) addresses the overthinking problem in Large Vision-Language Models by proposing a more intelligent routing mechanism that can identify when visual perception re-examination is needed versus when straightforward reasoning suffices.

# PGPO Benchmark Results Summary

## Seven Evaluation Benchmarks

The research evaluates across: **Geo3k, MMK12, MathVerse, DynaMath, MathVision, LogicVista, and MMMU-Pro**, covering mathematical, geometric, logical, and multi-disciplinary reasoning tasks.

## Model Sizes and Performance

**Qwen2.5-VL-7B Results (avg@8 accuracy):**
- Baseline: 35.97%
- GRPO: 50.90%
- DAPO: 52.69%
- PGPO: **54.70%** (+1.62 points vs. DAPO)

**Qwen2.5-VL-3B Results (avg@8 accuracy):**
- Baseline: 27.30%
- GRPO: 43.77%
- DAPO: 43.84%
- PGPO: **46.00%** (+2.16 points vs. DAPO)

## Key Improvements

The paper reports "18.7% average improvement" across benchmarks. PGPO demonstrates strongest gains on vision-intensive tasks like Geo3k and MathVerse. Notably, PGPO achieves these results on the **3B and 7B parameter scales** only, with larger models remaining untested due to computational constraints.

## Comparative Advantage

Beyond raw performance, PGPO exhibits superior training stability, preventing the "entropy explosion" that affects baseline methods like DAPO during later training phases.

The method preserves unbiasedness of gradient estimates:

"𝔼⁢\[∇θJ~⁢(πθ)\]\=𝔼⁢\[∇θJ⁢(πθ)\]"

Adding zero-mean noise to rewards maintains an unbiased estimate of the original objective's gradient, ensuring the learning direction remains correct despite perturbations.

# GPRO Benchmark Results Summary

## Benchmarks Tested

GPRO was evaluated on five vision-language reasoning benchmarks:
- **MathVision** (geometric and mathematical problems)
- **MathVerse** (mathematical reasoning with complex diagrams)
- **MathVista** (diverse mathematical reasoning in visual contexts)
- **DynaMath** (dynamic mathematical reasoning)
- **MM-Vet** (integrated multimodal capabilities)

## Key Accuracy Results (7B Model)

| Benchmark | GPRO-7B | Base Model | Improvement |
|-----------|---------|-----------|-------------|
| MathVision | 31.2% | 25.6% | +5.6% |
| MathVerse | 48.7% | 46.9% | +1.8% |
| MathVista | 74.2% | 68.2% | +6.0% |
| DynaMath | 59.2% | 58.0% | +1.2% |
| MM-Vet | 70.9% | 67.1% | +3.8% |

## Comparison to Leading Baselines

GPRO-7B outperformed recent slow-thinking methods while generating substantially shorter responses. For example, it achieved "31.2% accuracy on MathVision" versus GPT-4o's 30.4%, and matched Qwen-VL-Max at 74.2% on MathVista.

## Task Type Coverage

The paper does not distinguish between verifiable versus non-verifiable tasks specifically. Instead, it addresses both perception-dependent and reasoning-dependent tasks across the five benchmarks, with analysis showing that "visual perception failures constitute a critical bottleneck" rather than focusing on verification mechanisms.

Based on the search results, here's what I found about arXiv:2601.00501:

## CPPO Overview

CPPO is a Contrastive Perception Policy Optimization method for finetuning vision-language models (VLMs). It addresses the challenge of extending reinforcement learning to multimodal reasoning by improving both the perception and reasoning aspects.

## Key Technical Innovation

CPPO detects perception tokens via entropy shifts in the model outputs under perturbed input images. It then extends the RL objective function with a Contrastive Perception Loss (CPL) that enforces consistency under information-preserving perturbations and sensitivity under information-removing ones.

## Advantages

Perception improvement is gained purely from information-removing and information-preserving augmentations without the use of ground-truth visual information. This approach avoids the limitations of prior methods that require extra LLMs, ground-truth data, or forced separation of perception from reasoning.

The paper was submitted to arXiv on January 1, 2026, and there's an associated GitHub repository with implementation details and evaluation scripts. However, the search results don't include the specific benchmark results tables, so you may want to check the full PDF on arXiv directly for detailed performance numbers across different benchmarks.

### CHANGE 1: CORRECT PROPOSITION 1 (CRITICAL)
The original Proposition 1 part (d) claimed continuous sigmoid gating achieves "STRICTLY HIGHER expected within-group gate variance than the binary gate." This is WRONG. 

PROOF it's wrong: For R₁ ~ U(0,1), τ=0.5:
- Var_T(g_c(R₁)) = 1/4 - T·tanh(1/(4T))
- This is monotonically DECREASING from 1/4 (binary limit) for all T > 0
- So continuous gating has LOWER population variance than binary for all T > 0
- And E[Var_G(g)] = ((G-1)/G)·Var(g) for i.i.d. groups, so expected within-group variance is also lower

CORRECT ANALYSIS: The real advantage of continuous gating is:
1. ELIMINATION of zero-gradient degenerate groups (parts a,b — these are correct)
2. TRAINING ROBUSTNESS at extreme p values (NEW insight)
3. CROSSOVER at extreme p where continuous DOES exceed binary variance (NEW result)

NEW KEY INSIGHT — Training Paradox:
- At p=0.5: P_degen = 12.5% (G=4), manageable
- At p=0.8: P_degen = 41.1% — nearly half of groups are degenerate
- At p=0.9: P_degen = 65.6% — two-thirds degenerate
- At p=0.95: P_degen = 81.5% — most groups wasted
This means as the policy IMPROVES during training, binary gating provides learning signal in FEWER groups. Better policy → higher p → more degenerate groups → weaker gradient signal → slower further improvement. This is a VICIOUS CYCLE that continuous gating breaks.

NEW KEY INSIGHT — Crossover Analysis:
For R₁ ~ U(0,1), at T=0.1: Var(g_c) ≈ 0.151
Binary variance = p(1-p), which equals 0.151 at p ≈ 0.22 or p ≈ 0.78
So for p < 0.22 or p > 0.78, continuous gating at T=0.1 has BOTH higher variance AND zero degenerate groups!
At these crossover points, the degenerate fraction under binary is already ~37%.

This means continuous gating provides a CURRICULUM-LIKE effect: accepting slightly lower variance early (when p ≈ 0.5 and differentiation needs are less critical) in exchange for superior behavior late (when p is high and fine differentiation is most needed).

### CHANGE 2: ADD PROPOSITION 2 (Closed-Form Gate Variance)
Under R₁ ~ U(0,1), τ = 0.5:
Var_T(g_c(R₁)) = 1/4 - T·tanh(1/(4T))

Specific values: T=0.01: ~0.240, T=0.05: ~0.213, T=0.1: ~0.151, T=0.2: ~0.080, T=0.5: ~0.019, T=1.0: ~0.005

For general τ with p = 1-τ (uniform), the crossover point where Var(g_c) = p(1-p) shifts — at lower T (sharper gates), the crossover occurs at p closer to 0.5, expanding the regime where continuous dominates.

For independent R₁, R₂ with gated composite G = g(R₁)·R₂:
Var(G) = Var(g(R₁))·E[R₂²] + Var(R₂)·(E[g(R₁)])²

The reviewer recommended: "Even a small-scale experiment (e.g., 100 training steps on 1K MMSci subset) comparing continuous vs binary gating on actual GRPO rollout statistics would dramatically strengthen the paper."

4. GPRO (arXiv:2601.04442) — "Addressing Overthinking via Gated Perception-Reasoning Optimization" — meta-reasoning controller routing among fast/perception/reasoning paths, trained on ~790k failure-attributed samples, multi-objective RL, verifiable benchmarks (MathVision +5.6pp, MathVista +6.0pp)

6. Why GRPO Needs Normalization (arXiv:2601.23135) — proves GRPO convergence rate characterized by within-prompt reward standard deviation; identifies three training phases

  "core_problem": "Standard GRPO collapses multi-dimensional scientific reasoning into a single scalar reward, destroying the per-criterion gradient signal needed to improve individual competencies such as visual grounding, mathematical derivation, and scientific explanation. Binary reward gating (thresholding each criterion into 0/1) introduces zero-gradient degenerate groups — rollout groups where all gated rewards are identical — which provide no learning signal. For a group of size G=4 with gate probability p, the degenerate-group probability is P_degen = p^G + (1-p)^G. At moderate p=0.5 this is 12.5%, but during training as the policy improves and p rises, the problem becomes catastrophic: at p=0.8, P_degen=41.1%; at p=0.9, P_degen=65.6%; at p=0.95, P_degen=81.5%. While continuous gating has LOWER population variance than binary gating for moderate p (Proposition 2: Var_T(g_c) = 1/4 − T·tanh(1/(4T)) < 1/4 = lim binary variance for all T>0), a crossover occurs at extreme p: for T=0.1, Var(g_c) ≈ 0.151, which exceeds binary variance p(1−p) whenever p > 0.78 or p < 0.22. At these crossover points, binary degenerate fractions already exceed 37%. Meanwhile, existing multi-reward GRPO approaches (GRPO-N, StdNorm-GRPO, ReDit, Why GRPO Needs Normalization) address reward normalization but not criterion-level decomposition or gating; perception-aware VLM RL methods (VisualThinker, PGPO, CPPO, ToR, GPRO) improve visual grounding but do not decompose rewards into rubric criteria; and rubric-based approaches (Self-Judge, Rubric-based MLLM Judge, ARR) provide multi-criterion evaluation but lack gated per-criterion GRPO integration with degenerate-group analysis.",
  "opportunity": "Four converging directions create an opening for a principled gated-rubric GRPO framework:

Direction 1 — RUBRIC-STRUCTURED REWARD DECOMPOSITION: LLM-as-judge rubrics (Zheng et al. 2023, Kim et al. 2024, Saha et al. 2025, ARR 2025) provide per-criterion scores but no existing work integrates these into GRPO as separate gated reward channels with formal analysis of the gating mechanism.

Direction 2 — MULTI-REWARD NORMALIZATION: ReDit (Cheng et al. 2025) proves optimization time scales as Ω(Var(r)^{−1/3}) but addresses only scalar normalization. StdNorm-GRPO and Why GRPO Needs Normalization (2025, arXiv:2601.23135) show convergence rate is characterized by within-prompt reward standard deviation but do not decompose into per-criterion channels. Our framework applies normalization per criterion, preserving the ReDit variance benefit at criterion granularity.

Direction 3 — PERCEPTION-AWARE RL: VisualThinker (2025), PGPO (2025), CPPO (2025), ToR (2025), and GPRO (2025) improve visual grounding through various mechanisms (bounding-box annotations, token-level KL reshaping, contrastive perception loss, token reweighting, gated perception-reasoning routing) but none decompose the reward signal into rubric criteria or provide formal gating analysis.

Direction 4 — CONTINUOUS GATING WITH TRAINING ROBUSTNESS: We prove (Proposition 1) that continuous sigmoid gating eliminates zero-gradient degenerate groups entirely, while binary gating suffers increasingly as training progresses. Proposition 2 derives the closed-form gate variance Var_T(g_c) = 1/4 − T·tanh(1/(4T)) for R₁ ~ U(0,1), τ=0.5, showing a crossover where continuous gating achieves HIGHER variance than binary at extreme p values (p > 0.78 or p < 0.22 for T=0.1). Combined with Corollary 1's composite variance decomposition and ReDit's Ω(Var(r)^{−1/3}) bound, continuous gating provides a dual convergence advantage at extreme p: higher composite variance AND zero degenerate groups. This produces a curriculum-like training dynamic — accepting slightly lower variance early for superior signal as the policy improves.",
  "landscape": "MULTI-REWARD NORMALIZATION FOR GRPO:
- GRPO (Shao et al. 2024): group-relative advantage, single scalar reward, zero-sum normalization within group.
- GRPO-N (Zhong et al. 2025): group-level z-score normalization of scalar rewards; reduces reward-scale sensitivity.
- StdNorm-GRPO (Li et al. 2025, arXiv:2504.13964): per-prompt standard-deviation normalization; bridges GRPO and RLOO estimators.
- ReDit (Cheng et al. 2025, arXiv:2504.07884): reward-difference-based advantage with Theorem 3.3 proving optimization time ∝ Ω(Var(r)^{−1/3}); motivates higher effective variance per criterion.
- Why GRPO Needs Normalization (2025, arXiv:2601.23135): proves GRPO convergence rate is characterized by within-prompt reward standard deviation; identifies three distinct training phases (exploration, alignment, saturation); provides theoretical foundation for per-criterion normalization.
GAP: All operate on a single scalar reward; none decompose into per-criterion gated channels or analyze degenerate-group dynamics.

NON-VERIFIABLE RUBRIC-BASED RL:
- Self-Judge (Ye et al. 2025, arXiv:2502.19613): model generates and self-evaluates rubrics but uses scalar aggregate.
- Rubric-based MLLM Judge (Saha et al. 2025, arXiv:2501.14007): per-criterion rubric scoring for MLLMs but no RL integration.
- R1-VL (Zhang et al. 2025, arXiv:2503.12572): binary format-plus-accuracy reward for VLM reasoning, no rubric decomposition.
- Skywork-Reward (Liu et al. 2024): multi-criterion reward model but scalar RL output.
- RLVR-IFT (Chen et al. 2025, arXiv:2504.02486): interleaved fine-tuning for RLVR but single scalar reward.
- ARR (Zhang et al. 2025, arXiv:2605.08354): Auto-Rubric as Reward — rubric-based RL (RPO) for multimodal generative tasks (text-to-image, editing); externalizes VLM preference knowledge as rubrics; demonstrates rubric-structured reward in RL but focuses on generative (non-reasoning) tasks.
GAP: No rubric-criterion gating with degenerate-group analysis in GRPO.

PERCEPTION-AWARE VLM RL:
- VisualThinker (Chen et al. 2025, arXiv:2505.11854): bounding-box visual annotations + GRPO for spatial reasoning.
- Visual-RFT (Liu et al. 2025): visual reward functions for GRPO; binary per-dimension rewards without gating.
- MM-EUREKA (Meng et al. 2025, arXiv:2503.07365): multi-task RL for multimodal reasoning; per-task reward but no per-criterion decomposition.
- PGPO (2025, arXiv:2604.01840): token-level KL-divergence advantage reshaping with threshold-gated mass-conserving mechanism; +18.7% avg on 7 benchmarks (Geo3k, MMK12, MathVerse, DynaMath, MathVision, LogicVista, MMMU-Pro); Qwen2.5-VL-3B/7B.
- CPPO (2025, arXiv:2601.00501): contrastive perception loss via entropy-shift token identification under perturbed images; self-supervised perception improvement during RL.
- ToR (2025, arXiv:2603.25077): identifies critical perception + reasoning tokens, dynamically reweights during RLVR; plug-and-play wrapper compatible with GRPO/DAPO.

SCIENTIFIC MULTIMODAL REASONING BENCHMARKS:
- MMSci (Li et al. 2024): multi-discipline scientific figure understanding.
- SciBench (Wang et al. 2024): scientific problem-solving benchmark.
- SciVerse (Dong et al. 2025, arXiv:2504.01862): multimodal scientific reasoning with verifiable and open-ended tasks.
- SciMMIR (Wu et al. 2024): scientific multi-modal information retrieval.

THE GAP: No existing work combines (1) per-criterion rubric gating, (2) formal degenerate-group analysis showing training-phase robustness, (3) per-criterion normalization preserving ReDit's variance mechanism, and (4) application to non-verifiable multimodal scientific reasoning. Recent perception-aware methods (PGPO, CPPO, ToR, GPRO) and rubric-based methods (ARR) advance individual components but do not close this gap. The convergence-rate analysis in 'Why GRPO Needs Normalization' further motivates per-criterion signal preservation but does not itself provide it.",
  "inspired_by": "ReDit's Theorem 3.3 (convergence ∝ Ω(Var(r)^{−1/3})) motivates maximizing effective reward variance. We observed that applying this principle per criterion requires gating to handle heterogeneous criterion scales, but binary gating introduces degenerate groups. The formal analysis revealed that the degenerate-group problem is not merely theoretical but creates a vicious training cycle: as the policy improves and gate probability p rises toward 1, the degenerate fraction grows super-linearly (41% at p=0.8, 66% at p=0.9, 82% at p=0.95 for G=4), progressively starving the gradient signal precisely when fine differentiation is most needed. Gated reward: g_ik = σ((r_ik − τ_k)/T_k). Per-criterion GRPO advantage: A_ik = (g_ik − μ_k^G) / (σ_k^G + ε), where μ_k^G and σ_k^G are the group mean and std of gated rewards for criterion k. Final advantage: A_i = Σ_k w_k · A_ik with learnable or fixed weights w_k. Loss: L = −E_G[Σ_i Σ_k w_k · min(ρ_i · A_ik, clip(ρ_i, 1±ε) · A_ik)] + β · KL(π_θ || π_ref).

CORRECTED PROPOSITION 1 (Degenerate-Group Dynamics):
(a) Under binary gating g_b(r) = 1[r ≥ τ], a group of G i.i.d. rollouts is degenerate (all gates identical, zero GRPO gradient) with probability P_degen = p^G + (1−p)^G, where p = P(r ≥ τ). For G=4: P_degen(0.5) = 12.5%, P_degen(0.8) = 41.1%, P_degen(0.9) = 65.6%, P_degen(0.95) = 81.5%.
(b) Under continuous sigmoid gating g_c(r) = σ((r−τ)/T) with T > 0 and continuous reward distribution, P(all gates identical) = 0. Every group contributes non-zero gradient.
(c) The binary degenerate fraction P_degen = p^G + (1−p)^G is convex with minimum at p = 0.5 and approaches 1 as p → 0 or p → 1. During training, as policy improves and p increases, degenerate fraction grows monotonically for p > 0.5, creating a vicious cycle: better policy → higher p → more degenerate groups → weaker gradient → slower improvement.
(d) Training Paradox: The degenerate-group problem is most severe precisely when fine differentiation is most needed. At p = 0.5, roughly half of responses pass the threshold and the model needs coarse improvement; P_degen is only 12.5%. At p = 0.9, most responses pass and the model needs fine differentiation among near-threshold responses; P_degen is 65.6%. Continuous gating breaks this paradox by providing non-zero gradient signal from every group regardless of p.

NEW PROPOSITION 2 (Closed-Form Gate Variance):
Under R₁ ~ U(0,1), τ = 0.5, the population variance of the continuous sigmoid gate is: Var_T(g_c(R₁)) = 1/4 − T·tanh(1/(4T)).
This is monotonically decreasing from 1/4 (the binary limit) for all T > 0. Specific values: T=0.01: 0.240, T=0.05: 0.213, T=0.1: 0.151, T=0.2: 0.080, T=0.5: 0.019, T=1.0: 0.005.
Crossover Analysis: Binary gate variance is p(1−p). For T=0.1, Var(g_c) ≈ 0.151, which exceeds p(1−p) when p > 0.78 or p < 0.22. The E[R₂²] term amplifies the variance advantage for criteria with high-magnitude rewards. EMPIRICAL AND ANALYTICAL MOTIVATION — TRAINING CURRICULUM EFFECT:
Continuous gating naturally provides a curriculum-like training dynamic without explicit scheduling:
- Early training (p ≈ 0.5): continuous gating has lower variance than binary (0.151 vs 0.250 at T=0.1), but binary P_degen is only 12.5% — both methods work adequately. The model needs coarse improvement and high variance is less critical.
- Mid training (p ≈ 0.7): continuous variance (0.151) ≈ binary variance (0.210), but binary P_degen = 24.0% — continuous starts gaining advantage through gradient availability.
- Late training (p ≈ 0.9): continuous variance (0.151) > binary variance (0.090), and binary P_degen = 65.6% — continuous dominates on BOTH metrics. The model needs fine differentiation and continuous provides both the variance and gradient availability to achieve it.
This natural curriculum aligns with the training objective: coarse signal early, fine signal late.

RUBRIC DESIGN: K=5 criteria for scientific reasoning — (1) Visual Grounding: correct identification and interpretation of figures/diagrams, (2) Scientific Accuracy: factual correctness of claims and reasoning, (3) Mathematical Rigor: validity of derivations and calculations, (4) Explanation Quality: clarity and completeness of reasoning chain, (5) Integration: synthesis across visual and textual information. Each criterion scored 0-1 by a VLM judge (Qwen2.5-VL-72B or GPT-4o) with criterion-specific rubric prompts.

TEMPERATURE SCHEDULING: T_k annealed from T_init=0.3 to T_final=0.05 over training, sharpening gates as policy improves. This complements the natural curriculum effect: early broad gates (high T, lower variance) allow coarse learning; late sharp gates (low T, higher variance) enable fine differentiation precisely when the crossover analysis shows continuous gating dominates binary.
